title: The vine (John 15:1–8)
hook: abide in me; without me you can do nothing

segments.voice: Yesterday, eirene: peace given in the middle of trouble. Your line was not as the world gives.

Cut a rose for a vase and it looks perfect for a day or two. Same color, same petals, same smell as the one still on the bush. But it's already on a clock. It has everything except a connection. Nothing is flowing into it anymore. At the end of chapter fourteen Jesus says, arise, let us go hence. Some readers picture them leaving the supper room and walking out into the dark. John doesn't say where they are. What comes next is a vine.
screen: `A CUT ROSE, ON A CLOCK.` → `ARISE, LET US GO HENCE.` → `A VINE.`

segments.voice: It's another of John's I am sayings, and the Douay-Rheims begins: "I am the true vine; and my Father is the husbandman." Husbandman is the old word for farmer, the one who tends the vines. In the Hebrew scriptures, Israel itself is pictured as God's vine, planted and cared for. Jesus takes the picture personally. Then the key verse: "I am the vine; you the branches: he that abideth in me, and I in him, the same beareth much fruit: for without me you can do nothing." The word to hold is abide. In Greek it's menō, to stay, remain, live somewhere, and it shows up again and again in these few verses. A branch doesn't produce fruit by straining or trying harder. It stays attached, and the sap does the work. There's a hard note too: the farmer prunes. Every branch that bears fruit, he cuts back, so it bears more. Anyone who's watched a grapevine pruned in winter knows how brutal it looks, bare stubs where there were long canes, and how much fruit comes that summer. Catholics hear the vine in two places especially. One is the Eucharist, the fruit of the vine on the altar. The other is the ordinary day. Some saints recommended very short prayers through the day, sometimes called aspirations: a name or a single line, said while washing dishes or waiting at a light, like Jesus, Mary, Joseph. Not a long prayer. Just staying connected.
screen: `ANOTHER I AM: THE TRUE VINE.` · `ABIDE: STAY, REMAIN, LIVE.` · `THE FARMER PRUNES.` · `SHORT PRAYERS THROUGH THE DAY.` · then, large: `THE VINE.`

segments.voice: Notice where your body is held: feet on the floor, back against the chair, hands resting, and let your weight settle there. Don't try to do anything; just remain, and when your mind wanders, come back to those points of contact. If you pray, hold one short line from the Gospel, abide in me; if you don't, simply stay where you are.
The vine. Jesus is the vine and his followers the branches: whoever abides in him bears much fruit. Today's word.
Your line: abide. A branch doesn't strain to bear fruit; it stays. Day five hundred twenty, done.

howItsDone: Many Catholics pray short aspirations through the day, a name or a single line such as "Jesus, Mary, Joseph," alongside longer prayer at Mass and at home.

chat.says: What does Jesus mean by abide in me? Like, try harder?
options: No, stay connected. A branch doesn't strain to bear fruit; it stays on the vine.
Yes, work harder at being good, and he'll keep you on the vine.
It means pray for long hours, since short prayers don't really count.
chat.meaning: Abide, menō, means stay or remain. A branch bears fruit by staying attached, and the sap does the work.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the golden temple vine (not in the cited text), 'last of John's I am sayings' and the 'about ten times' count (hook, teach, screen, trapdoor); 'a long sermon' to 'a long prayer'; 'saints' to 'some saints'.
Golden vine on the temple gate: Josephus describes it (Antiquities 15.11.3; War 5.4.4); the hook marks the setting as a reader's guess. Confirm.
'About ten times in ten verses': count of menō in John 15:4–10 varies by counting; stated as 'about'. Verify.
'Last of John's great I am sayings' assumes the usual seven (bread, light, door, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine). Confirm.
Aspirations / ejaculatory prayers recommended by saints (e.g. Francis de Sales): stated generally. Confirm.
